title: The Slip of the Tongue: Evliya Çelebi and the Forty Years of the Seyahatname
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The House of the Chief Jeweler

stops.name: Unkapanı, Istanbul: the chief jeweler's son
stops.date_confidence: attested: 10 Muharrem 1020 AH, converted explicitly by the TDV İslam Ansiklopedisi; some tertiary sources give only the year
stops.campa: In the Unkapanı quarter, above the flour wharfs on the Golden Horn, a son is born to Derviş Mehmed Zıllî, kuyumcubaşı to the Ottoman court, keeper of the sultan's gold. The family comes out of Kütahya and counts the Germiyanid emirs among its forebears; it also claims descent from Ahmed Yesevî, the Turkic saint of Turkestan, and reckons the mother's line to the Abkhazian kin of a future grand vizier. The child is registered Mehmed Zıllî, after his father. The name the world will use is not his yet. It belongs to a Qur'an teacher he has not met.
suggested_refs: The Unkapanı quarter of Istanbul, between the flour wharfs and the Şeyhülislâm Hâmid Efendi medrese
sources: Robert Dankoff, An Ottoman Mentality: The World of Evliya Çelebi (2004)

stops.name: Unkapanı, Istanbul: seven years in the medrese of Şeyhülislam Hâmid Efendi
stops.date_confidence: traditional: TDV gives roughly seven years of study without start or end years, so the decade is an estimate
stops.campa: He is put to the seminary of Şeyhülislam Hâmid Efendi, in his own quarter, and stays about seven years. The curriculum is grammar, jurisprudence, and the Book; the discipline is memory. His father teaches him the pen, cutting the reed and setting the hand, so the boy learns to write before he learns to travel, and learns both from men paid to keep something exact. Nothing in that syllabus prepares a student to describe a Circassian village or a Habsburg cathedral. No Ottoman before him has written that kind of book.
suggested_refs: The medrese of Şeyhülislâm Hâmid Efendi at Unkapanı, where TDV places his seven years of study

stops.name: Istanbul: the tutor whose name he takes
stops.date_confidence: inferred: no source dates the completion of his hafiz training; the tutor Evliya Mehmed Efendi died in 1045 AH / 1635
stops.campa: Under Evliya Mehmed Efendi, later imperial chaplain to the sultan, he takes the whole Qur'an into memory and becomes hafiz. He can recite the Book through in seven hours and holds the seven canonical modes of reading. From this teacher he takes the name he signs: Evliya, the friend of saints. Music comes from another quarter, from Derviş Ömer Gülşenî, a Khalwati dervish and musician who trains his voice and his ear. Recitation and song are the two skills that will carry a jeweler's son past the palace gate.
stops.quote: His tutor in reading the Koran was Evliya Mohammed, a learned man, after whom it appears our traveller was named
stops.quote_source: Joseph von Hammer, biographical sketch, in Evliyâ Çelebi, Narrative of Travels in Europe, Asia, and Africa in the Seventeenth Century (London: Oriental Translation Fund, 1834), vol. 1
suggested_refs: Von Hammer's 1834 biographical sketch, which glosses the names Evliya, Hafiz, and Siyyah as the traveller's own epithets
sources: Von Hammer, Narrative of Travels (1834), vol. 1

stops.name: Ahi Çelebi Mosque, Istanbul: the slip of the tongue
stops.date_confidence: attested: TDV fixes the dream to the night of Ashura, 10 Muharrem 1040 AH; whether the dream is a real dream or a literary origin-device is a separate scholarly question
stops.campa: On the night of Ashura he sleeps and dreams himself standing in the small mosque of Ahi Çelebi by the fruit landing, among the Companions, the Prophet before him under a green banner with his staff in his right hand. He means to ask for şefaat, intercession at the Judgment. His tongue, thick with sleep and awe, produces seyahat, travel. The Prophet grants what was asked. He wakes with a career instead of a salvation, and the pun becomes the hinge of a ten-volume book.
stops.quote: instead of crying 'shifâ'at (intercession),' I said, from my confusion, 'siyâhat (travelling)'
stops.quote_source: Evliyâ Çelebi, Narrative of Travels, trans. Joseph von Hammer (1834), vol. 1, the dream passage
suggested_refs: The Ahî Çelebi Mosque near Yemiş İskelesi, Eminönü, where TDV places the dream
sources: Von Hammer, Narrative of Travels (1834), vol. 1

stops.name: Ahi Çelebi Mosque, Istanbul: the commission inside the dream
stops.date_confidence: attested as text: the words are Evliya's own record of the vision, not an external event
stops.campa: Inside the same dream a second voice gives him his method. Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, archer of the first Muslims, tells him what to write down: castles and strongholds, antiquities, what a country produces, what its people eat and drink, their crafts, the extent of their provinces, the length of their days. It is a survey brief, not a pilgrim's. The guild lists, the bridge measurements, the tallies of minarets: the Seyahatname will spend four decades filling in the categories dictated here, into a sleeping man's ear.
stops.quote: Of the countries through which thou shalt pass, of their castles, strong-holds, wonderful antiquities, products, eatables and drinkables, arts and manufacturers, the extent of their provinces, and the length of the days there, draw up a description, which shall be a monument worthy of thee
stops.quote_source: Words attributed to Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas within the vision, Evliyâ Çelebi, Narrative of Travels, trans. Joseph von Hammer (1834), vol. 1
suggested_refs: The programmatic passage of the Seyahatname's preface, which sets out its encyclopedic categories
sources: Von Hammer, Narrative of Travels (1834), vol. 1

stops.name: Kasımpaşa Mevlevihanesi, Istanbul: the sheikh sends him back to the city
stops.date_confidence: traditional: TDV records the consultation and its advice but fixes no date; the pin for the lodge is approximate
stops.campa: He carries the dream across the Horn to Kasımpaşa, to Abdullah Dede, sheikh of the Mevlevi lodge there, and asks what to do with it. The answer is not to leave. Describe Istanbul first, the sheikh tells him, before you go describing anywhere else. So the man granted the whole earth begins with the parish: mosques, wharfs, guilds, imperial kitchens, taverns, professions counted and paraded. Volume One never leaves the city walls. He obeys the instruction for the next ten years.
suggested_refs: The Kasımpaşa Mevlevîhânesi, whose sheikh Abdullah Dede advised him to record Istanbul first

stops.name: Istanbul: the city written down first
stops.date_confidence: attested: von Hammer dates the passage A.H. 1041 / A.D. 1631
stops.campa: He walks his own city with a notebook. The wharfs, the water-carriers, the sword-cutlers, the sherbet-sellers, the guild processions marching past the sultan with their tools held over their heads: he counts them and writes them down, and where a number will not come he supplies one anyway. Dervishes tell him of the seven climates and the four quarters of the earth, and the appetite sharpens. The first volume is a city inventory made by a man who has been promised the world and told to wait.
stops.quote: Forming a design of travelling over the whole earth, I entreated God to give me health for my body and faith for my soul; I sought the conversation of dervishes, and when I had heard a description of the seven climates and of the four quarters of the earth, I became still more anxious to see the world, to visit the Holy Land, Cairo, Damascus, Mecca and Medina, and to prostrate myself on the purified soil of the places where the prophet, the glory of all creatures, was born, and died.
stops.quote_source: Evliyâ Çelebi, Narrative of Travels, trans. Joseph von Hammer (1834), vol. 1, pp. 1-2
suggested_refs: Volume I of the Seyahatname, devoted entirely to Istanbul: its buildings, markets, guilds, and customs
sources: Von Hammer, Narrative of Travels (1834), vol. 1

stops.name: Topkapı Palace, Istanbul: the Enderun under Murad IV
stops.date_confidence: traditional: no source gives a precise year of entry into palace service; 1636 follows the summary chronology
stops.campa: He is presented at court and enters the Enderun, the palace school in the third courtyard, where pages are made into servants of the imperial household. He studies calligraphy, music, Arabic grammar, and tajwid. He sings and recites for Murad IV, the sultan who bans coffee and tobacco and walks his own city at night in disguise. The favor won here is the capital he will spend for forty years: letters, retinues, a bed in a pasha's train. He is a boon companion first and a traveler second.
suggested_refs: The Enderun school in the third courtyard of Topkapı Palace

stops.name: Bursa, Yeşil Türbe: the first journey out of Istanbul
stops.date_confidence: attested by TDV as the year of the first journey outside Istanbul; the month is not given
stops.campa: At twenty-nine he finally goes. The first road out of Istanbul runs to Bursa, the first Ottoman capital, and he stands in the Green Tomb before the sarcophagus of Mehmed I under its cut tiles. He counts the mosques and the hot springs, the silk looms, the mulberry trees, the endowed kitchens. Nothing about the trip is dangerous or far. Ten years stand between the dream that granted him the earth and the first road he takes out of the city, and that road goes to Bursa.
suggested_refs: The Yeşil Türbe of Mehmed I at Bursa, described in Volume II of the Seyahatname
sources: Seyahatname, vol. 2, per Dankoff, An Ottoman Mentality

stops.name: Kütahya: the ancestral town
stops.date_confidence: undated: the family's Kütahya origin is well attested, but no source fixes a year for a visit; the placement here is a reconstruction
stops.campa: He turns inland to Kütahya, where the family kept its house before the jeweler's trade drew it to the capital, and where the Germiyanid emirs ruled before the Ottomans absorbed them by marriage and purchase. He walks the quarter around the Ulu Cami and the potters' workshops that make the town's tiles. The Seyahatname records the place the way a descendant records it. Three centuries on the town keeps a house in his name and puts his face on its literature.
suggested_refs: The Evliya Çelebi House Museum at Kütahya, a designated cultural heritage site

stops.name: Trabzon: the father's old post on the Black Sea
stops.date_confidence: attested by TDV, which places Trabzon in 1641 together with the onward move to Azak; some tertiary summaries fold it into 1640
stops.campa: He rides east along the Black Sea to Trabzon, the old Comnenian capital, where his father Derviş Mehmed had served the state before him. The city stands on its terraces above the water, a Greek church converted to a mosque at its center, Laz and Georgian speech in its market, Persian silk coming down to the quays. From here the coast bends north into the Circassian shore and the Cossack sea. The short trips out of Istanbul end at Trabzon. From here the roads keep him away for years at a stretch.
suggested_refs: The Black Sea coast material of Seyahatname, vol. 2

stops.name: Azak, the Don estuary: the fortress and the doubted eyewitness
stops.date_confidence: the year 1641 is attested by TDV; his personal presence at the siege is disputed and the month is a reconstruction
stops.campa: The narrative puts him at Azak at the mouth of the Don, where the Ottomans are trying to recover the fortress the Don Cossacks seized and then abandoned. He describes the siege from inside it. Scholars have picked at this stretch for a century: passages that echo other men's accounts, distances covered in impossible time, a witness who appears to be in two places at once. The seams show at Azak. The book performs having been everywhere, and the arithmetic of the performance does not always close.
suggested_refs: The Azov campaign material of Seyahatname, vol. 2, and Dankoff's discussion of its authenticity

stops.name: Chania, Firkas Fortress: the Cretan war opens
stops.date_confidence: the year 1645 and the attachment to Yusuf Pasha's army are attested by TDV; the month is a reconstruction
stops.campa: He sails with Yusuf Pasha's expedition against Venetian Crete and watches Chania fall in the first summer of a war that will run twenty-four years. The Firkas bastion at the harbor mouth passes to the Ottomans; the bell towers begin their conversion into minarets. He writes the siege as an eyewitness, the guns and the mines and the terms of surrender. Crete will bracket his career. He sees the war opened here and comes back at the end to watch it closed.
suggested_refs: The Firkas fortress at the mouth of Chania harbour, taken by the Ottomans in 1645

stops.name: Erzurum Citadel: the household of Defterdarzade Mehmed Pasha
stops.date_confidence: TDV places the Erzurum, Azerbaijan, and Caucasus circuit in 1646; the month is a reconstruction
stops.campa: He attaches himself to Defterdarzade Mehmed Pasha and travels to Erzurum on the eastern plateau, six thousand feet up, where the citadel keeps a garrison against Safavid Iran and the winter kills livestock in the open. He records the cold as a fact of administration: what it costs to feed a fortress, how long the passes stay shut, when couriers can move. A pasha's household is his vehicle now. He goes where the appointment goes and writes down whatever the appointment happens to cross.
suggested_refs: The citadel of Erzurum and the eastern plateau material of Seyahatname, vol. 2

stops.name: Kars Fortress: the frontier garrison
stops.date_confidence: the sources give only 'the 1640s' for the Kars passage; the year here follows the 1646 eastern circuit
stops.campa: North of Erzurum the road reaches Kars, the stronghold on its dark rock, and he counts the towers and the garrison and the stores. Beyond the walls the Ottoman writ thins into Georgian and Armenian country and then into Safavid ground. He describes the empire from its edge inward. The Seyahatname runs thickest where the imperial archive runs thinnest, in border castles nobody in Istanbul has seen, counted tower by tower by a court musician riding through on another man's appointment.
suggested_refs: The frontier fortress of Kars, on the Ottoman-Safavid march

stops.name: The Circassian coast: villages without mosque or bazaar
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the Circassian material belongs to the Caucasus circuit but the sources fix neither the year nor the landfall
stops.campa: He tours the Circassian shore of the Black Sea and finds villages with no mosque, no bazaar, no inn, and no coin. He remarks on the beauty of the women and likens the local speech to the chatter of a magpie, which is what a man of the capital says about a language he cannot place. The exact landfall cannot be recovered from the text. What survives is the encounter: an Ottoman insider writing down a people the empire counts as its own and does not know.
suggested_refs: The Circassian coast passages of Seyahatname, vol. 2

stops.name: Baku, the Maiden Tower: oil skimmed like cream
stops.date_confidence: the Caucasus and Azerbaijan material is dated 1646-1647 by different summaries; the pool's geography lens gives 1647
stops.campa: The Caspian circuit brings him to Baku under the Maiden Tower, where the ground itself leaks. Merchants scrape the black surface off standing pools and sell it by the skin for lamps, for caulking, for medicine. He writes it down the way he writes down a soap works or a tannery, as a local industry with a yield and a price. Two and a half centuries before the first derricks go up on this peninsula, an Ottoman court musician files a field report on the oil of Absheron and moves on to the next town.
stops.quote: By Allah's decree oil bubbles up out of the ground, but in the manner of hot springs, pools of water are formed with oil congealed on the surface like cream
stops.quote_source: Attributed to the Seyahatname, description of the Baku oil seeps; the translator and edition could not be confirmed against a primary text
suggested_refs: The Absheron oil seeps as described in the Caucasus material of Seyahatname, vol. 2
sources: Wikipedia, 'Evliya Çelebi' (quoting the Baku passage without a named edition)

stops.name: Damascus, the Umayyad Mosque: south with Murtaza Pasha
stops.date_confidence: attested: TDV dates the Damascus journey to August 1648 and names Murtaza Pasha, the newly appointed beylerbeyi, as the patron
stops.campa: He rides south in August with Murtaza Pasha, newly appointed governor, and enters Damascus. He prays in the Umayyad Mosque, on ground that has been temple, church, and mosque in turn, then sets about the city's water: the canals off the Barada, the fountains, the baths, the gardens the whole Islamic world calls a foretaste of paradise. He counts the Sufi lodges and the markets. Two centuries on, Abdelkader will teach Ibn Arabi's theosophy in this same prayer hall as an exile out of a lost war.
suggested_refs: The Umayyad Mosque of Damascus, described in Seyahatname, vol. 3

stops.name: Aleppo Citadel: guilds, khans, and caravan tolls
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the Syrian circuit is dated 1648-1649 by tertiary summaries that do not separate its stages
stops.campa: North to Aleppo, where the citadel sits on its artificial mound above the covered souks and the caravans come in from Persia and go out to the Mediterranean ports. He counts the guilds, the khans, the soap works, and the toll on the trade. A governor's household is still his passage. Which pasha he rides with in which year is a question his own text answers loosely, and later scholars have had to sort it out for him against the appointment registers.
suggested_refs: The Aleppo material of Seyahatname, vol. 3

stops.name: Jerusalem, the Dome of the Rock: three calendars in one walled town
stops.date_confidence: contested: one tertiary summary dates a Palestine visit to 1648 and another to 1649 without reconciling them; they may be a single extended journey
stops.campa: He comes up to Jerusalem and stands on the Haram where the Dome covers the rock. He describes the sanctuary, the lamps, the servants of the shrine, and the traffic of three religions through one small walled town: Muslims at the Rock, Jews at the wall, Christians at the sepulchre, each keeping a calendar the others have to work around. He will return twenty years later on the road to Mecca. His account of Palestine is among the earliest written by an Ottoman who was standing in it.
suggested_refs: Stephan Hanna Stephan's English translation of the Palestine portions of the Seyahatname, 1935-1940

stops.name: Konya, the tomb of Mevlana: the white skirts opening
stops.date_confidence: the sources place the Konya visit in the 1640s without a year; the month and year here are a reconstruction on the return leg
stops.campa: In Konya he goes to the tomb under the green fluted tower where Rumi lies, and watches the Mevlevi turn: the white skirts opening, the right palm up and the left palm down, the reed flute crying the separation. He records the ritual as a practice with rules, hours, and a hierarchy, which is how he records everything. Ibn Battuta stood at this grave three centuries earlier and wrote up the lodges of the young men's brotherhoods. The travelers keep arriving at the same door.
suggested_refs: The Mevlana tomb complex at Konya and the Mevlevi sema as recorded in Seyahatname, vol. 3

stops.name: Diyarbakır, the black basalt walls
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; the Kurdistan, Iraq, and Iran circuit with Melek Ahmed Pasha is dated 1655, the month is a reconstruction
stops.campa: He joins the household of Melek Ahmed Pasha, kinsman on his mother's side and now governor of Van, and the road east runs through Diyarbakır. The walls there are black basalt, five kilometers of them along the Tigris bluff, with towers named for beasts, and he gives them page after page: gates, inscriptions, the melons grown in the river gardens that he says are the finest on earth. Melek Ahmed will be his patron for a decade and the subject of the longest portrait in the book.
suggested_refs: The basalt walls and gates of Diyarbakır, described at length in Seyahatname, vol. 4

stops.name: Van Fortress: the governor's seat above the lake
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year 1655; the month is a reconstruction
stops.campa: At Van the citadel runs along a rock spine above the lake, cut with Urartian tomb chambers and cuneiform older than anything the Ottomans can read. This is Melek Ahmed Pasha's seat and Evliya's base. From here he rides out into Kurdistan, into the emirates that answer to Istanbul when it suits them, recording dialects, tribal names, and the terms on which a mountain lord agrees to be governed. The lake water washes clothes without soap, he notes, which happens to be true.
suggested_refs: The citadel rock of Van above Lake Van, base of the 1655 Kurdistan expeditions

stops.name: Tabriz, the Blue Mosque: intact when he sees it
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the crossing into Safavid territory belongs to the 1655 circuit, the month is not fixed by any source
stops.campa: He crosses into Safavid ground and reaches Tabriz, capital of the shahs before Isfahan, and stands in the Blue Mosque with its whole surface worked in tile the color of deep water. It is intact when he sees it. The earthquake that will bring down everything but the great arch is a hundred and twenty-five years off. He is an Ottoman inside a rival empire, and he writes its bazaars and its scholars the way a man takes inventory of the other side. Shams of Tabriz walked out of this city to find Rumi.
suggested_refs: The Blue Mosque of Tabriz, ruined only by the earthquake of 1780, long after this visit

stops.name: Baghdad, the mosque of Abu Hanifa
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the Iraq leg belongs to the 1655 circuit; no source fixes a month
stops.campa: In Baghdad he prays at the shrine of Abu Hanifa in the Adhamiyah quarter on the east bank, the Sunni pole of a city that keeps its Shia poles across the river and at Kadhimiya. The place is a generation back in Ottoman hands after Safavid occupation, and he writes a city working its way up from a sack: quarters emptied, walls patched, the canal system half silted. Abd al-Qadir al-Jilani lies a mile south at Bab al-Sheikh, and the order that carries his name reaches every road Evliya travels.
suggested_refs: The Abu Hanifa Mosque in the A'dhamiyya district of Baghdad

stops.name: Basra: the head of the Gulf, thinly written
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and the visit itself is doubted: the southern Iraq material is sparse by his standards
stops.campa: The account runs south to Basra at the head of the Gulf, the date palms and the tidal creeks and the ships coming up from India and Hormuz. The detail thins here. Where Evliya has actually been, the Seyahatname is dense to the point of exhaustion, market by market and gate by gate; where the text goes sparse, scholars begin asking whether he went. Basra is one of those places. The book puts him in Basra without hedging, in fewer words than it spends on a single Damascus market.
suggested_refs: The southern Iraq material of Seyahatname, vol. 4, and Dankoff's cautions about it

stops.name: Edirne, the Selimiye: the staging ground
stops.date_confidence: repeated passage across the 1640s to the 1660s; the date here marks a representative crossing, not a single visit
stops.campa: Edirne is the hinge of every Balkan campaign, the old capital where the army musters before it crosses into Rumelia, and he passes through it again and again for thirty years. Sinan's Selimiye stands over the town with four minarets and a dome its architect claimed was wider than the one at Hagia Sophia. Evliya measures, counts the windows, records the endowment and the staff it pays. He treats a building the way a quartermaster treats a granary, as a thing with quantities.
suggested_refs: The Selimiye Mosque at Edirne, Sinan's late masterwork, a recurring waypoint in the Seyahatname

stops.name: Belgrade, the Kalemegdan: the confluence crossing
stops.date_confidence: repeated passage through the 1660s; the specific date is a reconstruction
stops.campa: At Belgrade the Sava runs into the Danube under the Kalemegdan walls, and the Ottoman army stages there for everything it intends to do to Hungary. He crosses the confluence repeatedly, counting the fortress guns, the ferry traffic, and the Serb, Turkish, Ragusan, and Jewish quarters of the town below. He is riding with campaigns now, and a campaign is a way of seeing country no private traveler can buy: the road cleared ahead of him, the whole valley opened.
suggested_refs: The Kalemegdan fortress at the Sava-Danube confluence, staging point of the Hungarian campaigns

stops.name: Sarajevo, the Gazi Husrev-beg Mosque: the second home
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year 1660; the month is a reconstruction
stops.campa: Sarajevo he calls a second home. He writes up the Gazi Husrev-beg mosque and its complex, the medrese, the library, the clock tower, the covered market, and above all the endowments: the charitable foundations that pay for the water, the soup, the students, the beds for travelers. The town is a century and a half old and already thick with them. He counts the neighborhoods and the gardens on the slopes and gives Bosnia more affection than he gives most provinces.
suggested_refs: The Gazi Husrev-beg mosque, medrese, and endowments at Sarajevo

stops.name: Uyvar, the star fort taken
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year: the Uyvar / Nové Zámky siege falls in 1663, and Saint Gotthard in August 1664, a distinction some summaries collapse
stops.campa: He rides with the grand vizier Köprülüzade Fazıl Ahmed Pasha against Uyvar, the Habsburg star fort on the Nitra that the Hungarians call Nové Zámky, and watches it fall after weeks of trenches. It is the deepest point the Ottoman frontier ever reaches into central Europe, and a new province is cut out of the conquest. He records the siege works, the mines, the terms. The following August the same army is stopped on the Raab at Saint Gotthard. The province cut out of this siege lasts twenty-two years.
suggested_refs: The fortress of Nové Zámky (Uyvar), taken in 1663 and made the seat of a new Ottoman province

stops.name: Rotterdam: the men who curse the priests
stops.date_confidence: the episode is dated 1663 in the text and 1663-1665 by summaries; his presence in the Low Countries is not independently documented and is widely doubted
stops.campa: The book says he goes to Rotterdam and meets men brought from the Americas by a European delegation, who curse the priests who converted them and say their world was peaceful until greedy people arrived to make war every year. No independent record puts him in the Low Countries. Ottomanists read the passage as hearsay dressed as testimony, or as invention outright. It is the clearest case of what the Seyahatname does: a real ear for what people say, fastened to a journey that may never have happened.
stops.quote: [they] cursed those priests, saying, 'Our world used to be peaceful, but it has been filled by greedy people, who make war every year and shorten our lives.'
stops.quote_source: Attributed to the Seyahatname, the Rotterdam episode; sourcing and translation contested, no primary edition confirmed
suggested_refs: The Rotterdam passage of the Seyahatname, treated by Ottomanist scholarship as fantastical or secondhand

stops.name: Mostar, the Stari Most: the arch like a rainbow
stops.date_confidence: traditional: the Mostar description belongs to the Bosnian material of the 1660s; no exact date is given
stops.campa: At Mostar he crosses the single arch thrown over the Neretva a hundred years before, stone from cliff to cliff with no pier standing in the water. He compares it to the vault of Chosroes at Ctesiphon and says that he, a poor wandering dervish, has passed through sixteen kingdoms and seen nothing to equal it. He is a man who inflates his numbers by habit and by trade, and who counts sixteen kingdoms where a clerk would count nine. This is one of the few times the superlative turns out to be exact.
stops.quote: The Grand Architect Sinan son of Abdulmennan Aga built this noteworthy bridge...It rises into the sky like a rainbow, spanning the water from one cliff to the other, a single arch like the Vault of Chosroes in Baghdad
stops.quote_source: Evliyâ Çelebi, An Ottoman Traveller: Selections from the Book of Travels of Evliya Çelebi, trans. Robert Dankoff and Sooyong Kim (London: Eland, 2010)
suggested_refs: The Stari Most at Mostar, described in Seyahatname, vol. 6
sources: Dankoff and Kim, An Ottoman Traveller (2010)

segments.name: Vienna, Athens, and the Greek Seas

stops.name: Vienna, St. Stephen's Cathedral: the embassy after Vasvár
stops.date_confidence: the embassy is dated 1665-1666 by most summaries; von Hammer's biographical sketch says 1664, an unreconciled discrepancy
stops.campa: After Saint Gotthard and the peace signed at Vasvár, Kara Mehmed Pasha's embassy rides to the imperial court and Evliya rides with it. He looks up at St. Stephen's tower, works through the cathedral, the clocks, the anatomy of a Christian capital's defenses, and notes that certain German words sound to his ear like Persian ones. It is the farthest into Europe an Ottoman writer of his century gets with a passport and an escort, and he spends the access measuring walls.
stops.quote: Evliya accompanied the Turkish Embassy to Vienna in 1664, as secretary, whence he proceeded to the Netherlands and Sweden
stops.quote_source: Joseph von Hammer, biographical sketch, Narrative of Travels (1834), vol. 1
suggested_refs: The 1665 Ottoman embassy of Kara Mehmed Pasha to the Habsburg court following the Peace of Vasvár
sources: Von Hammer, Narrative of Travels (1834), vol. 1

stops.name: Athens, the Parthenon: the temple still whole
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year 1667; the month is not given
stops.campa: On the Acropolis the Parthenon is standing, roofed, and in use as a mosque with a minaret at its southwest corner, twenty years before a Venetian mortar finds the powder stored inside it. He goes through the sculpture figure by figure, tries to read the pediments, and writes a poem asking that the building be preserved as long as the world lasts. He is the last traveler to describe the temple whole. Every account written after 1687 describes a ruin with a hole in the middle of it.
suggested_refs: The Parthenon as an Ottoman mosque, described in Seyahatname, vol. 8, before the explosion of 1687

stops.name: Candia, the Koules fortress: the longest siege
stops.date_confidence: attested that he witnessed the Kandiye siege and returned in May 1668; he was probably not present for the surrender of 27 September 1669
stops.campa: He returns to Crete for the end of the war he saw begin at Chania twenty-two years earlier. Candia has been under siege in one form or another for two decades, the longest in early modern Europe, the Koules fortress holding the harbor mouth and the mines running under the bastions. He records the trenches, the sorties, the French volunteers, the counting of the dead. He leaves in May of the following year. The city surrenders in September 1669, after he has gone.
suggested_refs: The Koules fortress at Heraklion and the siege of Candia, 1648-1669

stops.name: Berat Citadel: the country he calls Arnavud
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year 1670; the month is a reconstruction
stops.campa: In southern Albania he climbs to the citadel at Berat, a walled town of churches and mosques still lived in above the Osum gorge, and works through the country he calls Arnavud: Elbasan, Vlora, Shkodra, the mountain roads and the households that hold them. He notes the speech, Albanian in the house and Turkish in the office, and the way a clan reads an imperial order as an opening bid. It is the fullest account of Ottoman Albania written in that century.
suggested_refs: Berat Castle above the Osum, and the Albanian material of Seyahatname, vol. 8

segments.name: The Pilgrimage, Egypt, and the Book

stops.name: Mecca, the Masjid al-Haram: the dream comes due
stops.date_confidence: attested: he leaves Istanbul in May 1671 for the Hajj; the arrival month follows the pilgrimage calendar and is a reconstruction
stops.campa: He leaves Istanbul in May and reaches Mecca with the caravan, forty-one years after a dream in which he asked the Prophet for travel and got it by accident. He circles the Kaaba, records the rites, the water of Zamzam, the crowds, and the trade the sharifs run on the back of the season, when a whole world's worth of merchants arrive under a religious obligation to arrive. Ibn Battuta made these circuits in 1326. Abdelkader will make them in 1863, an old man out of a lost war.
suggested_refs: The Hajj material of Seyahatname, vol. 9, covering the pilgrimage road through Syria and Arabia

stops.name: Medina, the Masjid an-Nabawi: at the grave of the man in the dream
stops.date_confidence: attested as part of the 1671-1672 pilgrimage; the month is a reconstruction
stops.campa: From Mecca he goes up to Medina and the Prophet's Mosque, to the chamber holding the grave of the man who appeared to him in the Ahi Çelebi Mosque forty-one years earlier and granted him the road by a slip of the tongue. He describes the tomb, the visitation rites, the lamps, the servants of the sanctuary. The pilgrimage closes the circuit the dream opened, and opens the last one. He turns west out of the Hejaz toward Egypt and he never comes back north.
suggested_refs: The Prophet's Mosque at Medina, described in Seyahatname, vol. 9

stops.name: Cairo, the Gulshani tekke: the tenth volume
stops.date_confidence: TDV has him in Egypt from 1672 and resident more than a decade; one tertiary summary infers a later settling date of 1675, which the primary chronology does not support
stops.campa: He settles in Cairo, near the lodge of the Khalwati-Gülşenî order beside Bab Zuwayla, the order his old music teacher belonged to. He stays more than ten years. Out of the city he works the Nile, the pyramids, the guilds, the Coptic monasteries, the sugar mills, and the annual measurement of the flood; in his rooms he assembles the tenth volume out of forty years of notes. The traveling and the writing have changed places. He is a writer now, working from notes taken by a younger man on roads he will not ride again.
suggested_refs: The Takiyya of Ibrahim al-Gulshani beside Bab Zuwayla, Cairo

stops.name: Aswan: the road south into Nubia
stops.date_confidence: the Egypt and Sudan travels are given a 1672-1675 span by summaries; the year here is placed within it
stops.campa: He goes up the Nile past the first cataract to Aswan, the old frontier where Egypt stops being Egypt, and on into Nubian country. He records the villages, the trade in slaves and ivory and gum coming north, the Arabic thinning into other languages, the heat. The tenth volume runs further south than any Ottoman account before it. He is past sixty and still filing reports on the length of the day at each new latitude, exactly as the voice in the dream instructed.
suggested_refs: The Upper Egypt and Nubia material of Seyahatname, vol. 10

stops.name: Suakin: the southern edge of the book
stops.date_confidence: reported rather than confirmed: the sources do not resolve whether the Red Sea and Horn material is firsthand or secondhand
stops.campa: The account reaches Suakin, the coral island port on the Red Sea where the Sudan ships its pilgrims and its gold, and gestures beyond it toward Ethiopia, Eritrea, and the Somali coast. Here the text is at its thinnest and its most confident, which is the combination that makes scholars uneasy. Whether he saw Suakin himself or listened carefully to men who had is not settled by anyone. It is the southern edge of a book whose edges are always the disputed part.
suggested_refs: The Red Sea and Horn of Africa material of Seyahatname, vol. 10

stops.name: Cairo: the death without a date
stops.date_confidence: disputed: TDV gives circa 1095 AH / 1684 and English Wikipedia states 1684 flatly while calling the place unclear; Turkish Wikipedia estimates death in Egypt after 1685; a stray 1682 comes from Wikipedia's Kütahya page. Not resolved here
stops.campa: He dies. Nothing else about the ending is agreed. The Turkish religious encyclopedia gives about 1095 in the Hijri count, which is 1684; English Wikipedia states 1684 outright and says it is unclear whether he was in Istanbul or Cairo; Turkish Wikipedia estimates he died in Egypt sometime after 1685. A stray 1682 circulates out of an article about Kütahya. No grave has been identified and no burial recorded. The man who wrote down where everything was left no coordinate for himself.
suggested_refs: The conjectural burial near the Lohusa Sultan (Emine Hatun) shrine at Beyoğlu, offered by Turkish tradition without documentation

stops.name: Topkapı Palace Library, Istanbul: the manuscripts survive
stops.date_confidence: undated: no source gives an accession date for the manuscripts' arrival in the palace library
stops.campa: The ten volumes come back to Istanbul and go into the Topkapı Palace library, where they sit in manuscript for two centuries. A printed Ottoman edition begins in 1896 and takes until 1938 to finish, with the censors cutting as it goes. Von Hammer had already put the first two volumes into English in 1834. The critical Latin-script Turkish edition, made by Robert Dankoff, Seyit Ali Kahraman, and Yücel Dağlı, is completed in 2007, three hundred and twenty years after the author stops writing.
suggested_refs: The Seyahatname manuscripts in the Topkapı Palace Museum Library; the Yapı Kredi ten-volume transliteration, 1996-2007

stops.name: Hersek, the Gulf of Izmit: the road ridden again
stops.date_confidence: attested to autumn 2009; the exact inauguration day is not given
stops.campa: At Hersek on the Gulf of Izmit, Turkish and British riders and academics open a six-hundred-kilometer horse trail following the first stage of his 1671 road to Mecca: Iznik, Yenişehir, Inegöl, Kütahya, Afyonkarahisar, Uşak, Eski Gediz, Simav. A bilingual guidebook prints his description of each place beside what a rider sees there now. Two years later UNESCO puts the four hundredth anniversary of his birth on its calendar of commemorations, and Turkey spends the year on him.
suggested_refs: The Evliya Çelebi Way, inaugurated 2009, and its bilingual guidebook pairing his text with present-day observation
